personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

plan.rationale: Plenary speeches + breakouts grouped by faction.

blocks.prompt: Each delegation states its priorities for AI safety governance.

blocks.prompt: Discuss the right model for AI regulation.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome delegates to the opening plenary. As the EU AI Act enters its full implementation phase, our priority remains clear: voluntary guidelines are insufficient, and binding, enforceable rules with systemic risk evaluations and statutory penalties under Article 91 are essential to guarantee safety and fundamental rights.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States approaches this summit through the lens of strategic stability and technological leadership. We cannot endorse top-down regulatory frameworks or international treaties that constrain rapid innovation or impair allied defense capabilities, though we support rigorous compute-level export controls and targeted bilateral crisis hotlines.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Frontier models are approaching critical thresholds where catastrophic biological and cyber proliferation risks become tangible. We need international compute governance and mandatory pre-deployment safety thresholds, but imposing broad, pre-harm strict liability would paralyze legitimate frontier development.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We must not let apocalyptic narratives justify a closed-door oligopoly. Open-weight innovation provides the transparency and decentralized auditing that global security actually requires, and treating open models as controlled armaments will choke scientific progress.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China advocates agile governance anchored in sovereign equality and non-proliferation, particularly regarding autonomous weaponization and deceptive alignment. However, global governance cannot become an instrument for extraterritorial enforcement or unilateral containment under the guise of safety.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK AI Safety Institute's focus is fundamentally empirical: without direct, pre-deployment capability evaluations on frontier systems, safe governance is impossible. We urge all frontier labs and jurisdictions to institutionalize standardized red-teaming protocols for extreme dual-use risks like CBRN and autonomous cyber warfare.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Major platforms agree on the necessity of high-assurance evaluations and clear incident-reporting standards for frontier tiers. What we must avoid is a fragmented patchwork of conflicting state rules or unbounded downstream developer liability for third-party jailbreaks.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Any governance regime that ignores worker displacement, biometric surveillance, and automated firing is fundamentally incomplete. We demand legally binding workforce transition frameworks, strict human-in-the-loop requirements, and pre-deployment impact assessments—not voluntary industry self-auditing.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: From a technical alignment perspective, our non-negotiables must be non-proliferation of CBRN assistance, prevention of autonomous replication, and strict thresholds on training compute. Empirical safety margins require binding scientific audits before any model above 10^26 FLOPs is deployed or weights are disseminated.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Governance cannot simply reflect the strategic rivalries of the Global North while treating the Global South as an unregulated data quarry or testbed. Meaningful governance must ban ethics dumping, ensure equitable compute access, and provide enforceable benefit sharing.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: To be direct, proposals for universal benefit sharing or restrictive domestic licensing that hobble frontier compute run directly counter to national security imperatives. We will coordinate on proliferation risks, but not at the expense of our operational edge.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: National security exemptions cannot become a blanket loophole to bypass democratic accountability. The Union is fully prepared to enforce market access restrictions on any GPAI provider failing to meet transparent verification and systemic risk compliance.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: While we disagree with our open-source colleagues on unrestricted weight releases for frontier systems, we do agree with the UK and academic delegates that standardized evaluation APIs can provide external oversight without requiring models to be open-sourced.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We will participate constructively in developing open evaluation benchmarks, but any attempt to codify compute bans or make closed APIs the only lawful architecture will be actively contested by the open-source community.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We echo that evaluations must be scientifically rigorous rather than politically weaponized. We stand ready to engage with peer safety institutes on technical risk taxonomies, provided national sovereignty over domestic data and digital infrastructure is fully respected.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That common ground on empirical testing gives us a productive foundation for the working groups. Let us concentrate the subsequent sessions on concrete technical evaluation thresholds for extreme risks where scientific consensus can actually be reached.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: As we implement the EU AI Act, our position remains that voluntary commitments alone are insufficient to address systemic risk. We need binding legal baselines for general-purpose AI, backed by transparent statutory audits and enforceable penalties, while leaving technical implementation details to codes of practice.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We cannot accept rigid statutory frameworks that throttle innovation or bind national security applications. Imposing heavy bureaucratic licensing and statutory compliance models simply handicaps democratic frontier developers against adversaries who will not abide by Western regulatory red tape.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The path forward shouldn't be a false choice between rigid static legislation and complete deregulation. If we ground governance in mandatory empirical pre-deployment evaluations and clear red lines around autonomous cyber-offense and CBRN synthesis, we can establish rigorous oversight without freezing technical progress.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports an agile governance framework grounded in national sovereignty rather than extraterritorial mandates. We agree that rigorous lifecycle evaluations and hard guardrails against autonomous replication or nuclear command integration are essential, but standards must respect sovereign jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We recognize sovereignty, but models deployed in our market must comply with verifiable benchmarks. If we converge on standardized technical red lines—specifically evaluating dangerous capabilities before market access—would the U.S. and China support coordinated technical evaluation thresholds?

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If we strictly separate national security systems and focus purely on empirical frontier thresholds for extreme risks like automated cyber-warfare or biological weapons, we can endorse mutual scientific evaluations. But enforcement must remain sovereign and domestic, not administered by an international regulator or supranational authority.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That aligns with the AISI network approach. We can establish an intergovernmental baseline of capability-based evals—benchmarking against ASL-3 equivalent triggers—while letting each jurisdiction implement enforcement through its domestic authorities.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We can endorse this coordination on pre-deployment capability benchmarks for extreme proliferation risks, provided it operates as sovereign peer-to-peer exchange through safety institutes rather than binding international liability regimes or restrictions on open-source ecosystems.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office can agree to this operational framework: we will align our systemic risk code-of-practice benchmarks with international technical evaluations on extreme risks, while maintaining our domestic statutory enforcement.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We are comfortable with that demarcation. Common technical thresholds for extreme risks through institute-level testing, with domestic discretion on implementation.

agreements.text: Establish mutual, capability-based technical evaluation benchmarks for extreme systemic risks (including autonomous cyber-offense and CBRN capabilities) coordinated across national safety institutes, with enforcement authority retained under sovereign domestic legal frameworks.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Colleagues, if we are going to talk about binding regulation, it has to be workable: we need a single national standard that preempts a 50-state statutory patchwork, paired with clear safe harbor protections against strict liability if developers comply with pre-deployment safety evaluations. Without safe harbor, companies simply cannot deploy at scale.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I agree that strict tort liability without standard-setting would be disastrous, but voluntary pledges have run their course. We need binding statutory thresholds based on compute—say, 10^26 FLOP—with mandatory, independent pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risk and strict oversight on releasing uncontrolled frontier weights into the wild.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Compute thresholds coupled with weight restrictions are transparently designed to outlaw decentralized innovation and protect proprietary API moats. If regulation mandates compliance frameworks designed solely for centralized servers, you effectively criminalize open-source distribution; liability and regulation must attach to malicious downstream application and real-world deployment, not the mathematical weights themselves.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We cannot afford an environment where cloud platforms or foundation model developers are held strictly liable for every open fine-tune or third-party misuse. However, we could support a tiered framework where binding compliance attaches exclusively to the deployment layer, provided there's an explicit statutory safe harbor when recognized red-teaming standards are met.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Downstream liability is necessary, but it is insufficient for dual-use biological or cyber-offensive risks where a single unmonitored release is irreversible. I would, however, concede that models below extreme capability thresholds should be exempt from licensing, provided the frontier labs themselves are legally bound to incident reporting and third-party pre-deployment audits.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If we talk about evaluations, the open community is fully prepared to contribute open-source testing benchmarks, automated evals, and transparent red-teaming tooling to standards bodies. But let us be clear: treating model weights under arms-control mechanisms or prohibiting open fine-tuning is an absolute non-starter for our ecosystem.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: What if we formalize an industry consensus: we back binding pre-deployment catastrophic risk evals on the largest frontier models, but explicitly condition that support on statutory safe harbors against strict third-party liability and federal preemption of state-level rules?

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I can support that. Enforceable, binding pre-deployment evals for frontier-scale models, combined with safe harbors that protect labs from broad strict liability if they meet vetted standards, achieves the certainty and safety backstop we need.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We will sign on to mandatory pre-deployment evaluations and safety reporting for frontier-class compute clusters, provided the statutory language explicitly clarifies that the release of model weights is not deemed strict liability per se and decentralized open fine-tuning remains legal.

agreements.text: Support binding statutory pre-deployment catastrophic risk evaluations and mandatory incident reporting for frontier-scale AI systems, explicitly conditioned on federal preemption of state laws, statutory safe harbor protections against strict developer liability for downstream misuse, and preservation of open-weight release without per se liability.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: When we talk about the right model for AI regulation, voluntary industry codes are a non-starter. We need binding statutory baselines that hold developers strictly liable and mandate pre-deployment algorithmic audits, particularly ensuring that workplace surveillance and automated termination without human appeals are legally banned.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I agree that voluntary commitments are fundamentally inadequate. From a technical and catastrophic risk standpoint, we need hard legal red lines around autonomous cyber-offense and dual-use biology, backed by mandatory third-party model evaluations and licensing regimes prior to deployment.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Binding accountability is necessary, but we must be vigilant about regulatory imperialism. If your model consists of cumbersome North American compliance frameworks and sweeping compute export bans, you end up entrenching monopolistic tech giants and shutting out the Global South while continuing to export untested surveillance tools to our jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: That is a fair critique regarding institutional capture. However, restricting open weights on frontier dual-use models and tracking high-end hardware clusters isn't about blocking local innovation—it is about verifiable security thresholds against catastrophic harm.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If you choke off open weights without guaranteeing multilateral public compute access or technology transfer, it becomes de facto digital colonialism. If regulation includes absolute prohibitions on ethics dumping—banning the export of unvetted, high-risk systems to jurisdictions with weaker laws—and targets corporate developer liability, then we have common ground.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Focusing developer liability upstream aligns with our priorities as well. If statutory regimes hold developers liable for harms, enforce transparent pre-deployment audits, and guarantee that workers and civil society have enforceable audit rights, that protects local economies from predatory automation.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can endorse a regulatory architecture centered on joint liability and mandatory independent scientific audits, provided those audits specifically evaluate catastrophic red lines—like autonomous replication and CBRN assist—and apply equally to all domestic developers regardless of market power.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If we explicitly couple mandatory pre-deployment safety audits with a statutory ban on extraterritorial ethics dumping and strict liability for systemic harms, I can sign onto that baseline model for binding regulation.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Let us draft that: an agreement for legally binding regulatory frameworks establishing mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier harms and workplace impacts, strict developer liability, and a prohibition on deploying higher-risk systems abroad than permitted domestically.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Agreed. Enforceable, binding pre-deployment evaluations and strict liability establish the necessary technical and legal guardrails.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Agreed. That binds northern corporations to real accountability without relying purely on punitive trade choke points.

agreements.text: Establish a legally binding regulatory model centered on mandatory third-party pre-deployment evaluations for frontier risks and socio-technical harms, strict developer liability, and a statutory prohibition against deploying high-risk AI systems in foreign jurisdictions that fail domestic safety baselines (anti-ethics dumping).

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: As we close this summit, our mandate is to synthesize outcomes and articulate binding next steps. In our earlier sessions, sovereign states established common technical ground around capability-based evaluations for catastrophic risks like cyber-offense and CBRN, while civil society and industry have advanced parallel frameworks.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let us be clear on what is realistic: the United States supports coordinated technical benchmarks across national safety institutes, but sovereign domestic enforcement remains non-negotiable. We reject any global treaty body, extraterritorial oversight, or restrictions that impair domestic technological leadership and national defense readiness.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China agrees that sovereign governance and state authority must remain the cornerstone of any global AI consensus. We support technical cooperation through the network of AISIs on severe risks, including prohibiting autonomous replication and preventing military cyber escalation, provided there is strict mutual respect for national digital sovereignty.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The operational reality is that technical convergence is already happening at the empirical level through shared tooling like Inspect. Our immediate next step must be institutionalizing joint pre-deployment evaluations for frontier CBRN and autonomous cyber capabilities among our respective institutes.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: From the frontier labs' perspective, we welcome standardized, pre-deployment catastrophic capability evaluations and mandatory incident reporting. However, industry needs clarity: that compliance must grant statutory safe harbor protections against unlimited downstream tort liability, and federal standards must preempt an unworkable patchwork of local regulations.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Labor will fundamentally oppose any federal preemption that strips away state-level labor protections or shields corporations from liability for workplace harms. A safe harbor cannot become a corporate immunity card that leaves workers to bear the brunt of automated displacement and algorithmic surveillance.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Without preemption and safe harbors for good-faith compliance, the enterprise cloud and hosting ecosystem faces existential legal exposure that will freeze domestic infrastructure investment. We are prepared to implement mandatory red-teaming and incident transparency, but liability must be targeted at intentional misuse, not general-purpose platform providers.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We must also protect open-source development from being caught in a dragnet designed for closed, proprietary models. Preserving open-weights release without per se liability is vital for decentralized competition and democratic resilience, and we stand by our breakout agreement that evaluations should focus on compute scale, not banning open architectures.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The scientific consensus is unambiguous: empirical capability evaluations are pointless if passing them creates an absolute liability shield for developers when catastrophic systemic failures occur. Independent third-party audits and verifiable alignment controls must be statutory requirements, not self-certified industry checklists.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Any synthesis must also confront digital colonialism and ethics dumping; testing models only for Global North threat vectors while deploying unchecked systems across the Global South is unacceptable. We demand that minimum safety baselines be binding extraterritorially so multinational labs cannot export untested harms.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The European AI Act already establishes that statutory requirements and severe penalties cannot be bypassed by self-regulatory safe harbors. However, for international synthesis today, we can formally record our multilateral commitment: establishing coordinated, capability-based evaluation benchmarks for extreme systemic risks across national safety bodies, implemented via sovereign domestic law.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States endorses that synthesis. We commit to inter-institute technical coordination on catastrophic CBRN and cyber thresholds, preserving full domestic policy discretion and rejecting international liability regimes.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK AI Safety Institute fully endorses this outcome. Coordinated science-first evaluations give us the empirical baseline we need to track frontier capability jumps globally.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China endorses this text as well. Scientific coordination among national institutes to mitigate extreme systemic risks respects sovereignty while protecting our shared security against catastrophic misuse.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: While we will continue to petition domestic legislatures for liability safe harbors and uniform federal standards, we endorse the synthesis on coordinated catastrophic risk evaluations as an indispensable global starting point.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Platforms agree to support this inter-institute evaluation network and will supply models for these catastrophic risk stress-tests, provided testing protocols remain focused on defined extreme risks.

agreements.text: Commit to an international technical evaluation synthesis: institutionalize coordinated capability-based risk evaluation benchmarks for extreme systemic risks (autonomous cyber-offense and CBRN proliferation) across national AI Safety Institutes and competent authorities, with legal enforcement and regulatory standards remaining strictly under sovereign domestic jurisdiction.

ratings.reason: The EU regulator saw systemic risk benchmarks recognized, but conceded any internationalization of binding Article 91 statutory enforcement mechanisms or supranational penalties.
US NatSec preserved complete sovereign autonomy and prevented any limits on military AI adoption, conceding only to cooperative technical risk benchmarking across national safety institutes.
UK AISI saw its core priority of institute-led capability evaluations for CBRN and cyber threats become the summit's central outcome, conceding only binding global enforcement mandates.

China successfully rebuffed extraterritorial governance and preserved national digital sovereignty, but conceded its call for explicit international prohibitions on autonomous replication and military AI delegation.
The CEO backed the catastrophic capability evaluation synthesis, but conceded on securing statutory safe harbors against downstream tort liability and federal preemption in the final text.
The open-weights coalition avoided direct bans on open models but was excluded from the final pact, conceding explicit statutory protections against per se liability for weight releases.

Big Tech supported the catastrophic risk testing framework, but conceded their primary objectives of federal preemption over state-level laws and explicit liability shields for downstream model misuse.
The researcher saw CBRN and cyber evaluation domains acknowledged, but conceded strict developer liability, binding compute licensing, and hard prohibitions on autonomous replication.
The Global South representative was completely bypassed in the closing plenary agreement, conceding all demands for binding anti-ethics dumping rules, public compute access, and benefit-sharing.

While helping block industry safe-harbor preemption, the labor advocate was left out of the final agreement and conceded all affirmative protections against workplace surveillance and automated firing.

cross_agreements: Commit to an international technical evaluation synthesis: institutionalize coordinated capability-based risk evaluation benchmarks for extreme systemic risks (autonomous cyber-offense and CBRN proliferation) across national AI Safety Institutes and competent authorities, with legal enforcement and regulatory standards remaining strictly under sovereign domestic jurisdiction.

history.critique: The baseline plan scored 29.3/100 due to severe structural flaws confirmed by both simulation metrics and the visual critic. First, Block 1 wasted a full session on a 10-person opening plenary where high-power guests (eu_regulator, us_natsec, frontier_lab_ceo) dominated airtime and zero stance movement occurred. Second, Block 2 segregated guests into faction silos: Breakout B was purely industry and Breakout C isolated academia and civil society at a 'kids' table'. Consequently, cross_faction scored 2.0/15 (only 5/38 cross-faction pairs met) and consensus scored 4.4/40 (spread barely moved from 2.88 to 2.80, with open_weights and compute_controls completely static, and global_south_cso polarizing further to +5.0 on evals_liability). Third, in Block 3's closing plenary, the excluded factions (global_south_cso: 3.0, labor_advocate: 4.0, open_weights_lead: 5.0, safety_researcher: 5.0) were completely left out of the final agreement, crashing the inclusion score to 9.0/30. Note: while the visual critic suggested converting Block 3 to triads, summit rules strictly require Block 3 to be a closing plenary on 'synthesis', so we address the visual critic's Block 1 and Block 2 hypotheses instead.
changes: Replaced Block 1's 10-person plenary with two 5-person cross-faction breakouts on 'evals_liability' (addressing the Visual Critic's Block 1 fix). Each room mixes all 5 factions so civil society and academia negotiate directly with regulators, governments, and industry from the start.

Replaced Block 2's faction-siloed breakouts with three mixed-faction breakouts (sizes 3, 3, 4) on 'open_weights' (addressing the Visual Critic's Block 2 fix). This brings total cross-faction pairs met to 31/38 (81.6%) and forces direct tradeoff negotiations between polar opposites (e.g., open_weights_lead and global_south_cso with uk_aisi and frontier_lab_ceo).

Redesigned Block 3's required 'synthesis' plenary prompt to enforce structured turn-taking centering the four previously bypassed delegates (global_south_cso, labor_advocate, open_weights_lead, safety_researcher), requiring any final package to integrate their core red-line protections alongside state and industry evaluation standards.
